title: Convex Analysis of Relaxation Dynamics in Chemical Reaction Networks and Generalized Gradient Flows
abstract: We obtain bounds on the Kullback--Leibler divergence to equilibrium for mass-action chemical reaction networks (CRNs) with equilibrium. The associated trajectory-dependent bounds are characterized in terms of the singular values of the stoichiometric matrix, convexity parameters, and time-integrated activities via deformed-exponential-type functions. We further extend these bounds within a generalized gradient flow framework. We highlight the biological relevance of this framework: the resulting bounds apply to quasi-steady-state regimes, where long transients and plateau-like behavior are common and functionally important. We illustrate the framework using a catalytic CRN exhibiting plateaus, where the bounds provide an a posteriori characterization of slow relaxation induced by local convexity and provide a bound-based approach to quantifying relaxation in CRNs.
comment: 34 pages, 5 figures (Main Text); 11 pages, 5 figures (Supplementary Material). Accepted for publication in SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics

title: A Multiscale Kinetic Model of DNA Damage Signalling and Repair under Combined Proton and Nanoparticle Exposure
abstract: We present a multiscale kinetic framework for predicting the induction, processing, and biological consequences of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in AG1522 human fibroblasts exposed to combined proton and 15-nm GNP irradiation. The model connects proton dose and linear energy transfer (LET), perinuclear GNP localization, secondary-electron and reactive-species production, and Poisson--Gamma-distributed lesion induction. Initial DSBs are separated into simple and complex classes and coupled to an ATM--$γ$H2AX--53BP1 signalling cascade, cell-cycle-dependent allocation among canonical non-homologous end joining, homologous recombination, alternative end joining, and single-strand annealing, and class-specific repair fidelities. The model identifies the initial complex-lesion fraction and its slower resolution, rather than post-irradiation conversion of simple DSBs, as the principal determinants of persistent damage under high-LET, GNP-enhanced irradiation. The residual-DSB results provide strong internal out-of-sample validation of the kinetic component. However, the opposing biases in correct repair and misrepair reveal an inconsistency between the class-specific fidelities and the supplied integrated-fidelity endpoint. These repair-fate predictions should therefore be regarded as model-constrained estimates pending independent measurements of correct-end joining, mutation, chromosome aberrations, and clonogenic survival.

title: A Central Limit Theorem for the Driver Site Frequency Spectrum
abstract: We consider a supercritical two-type continuous-time linear birth-death process with mutation and selection, in which wild-type individuals give rise to mutant offspring with a larger net-growth rate. We previously had obtained first-order law of large number results for the driver site frequency spectrum. We return to obtain a second-order central limit theorem, in which we show stable convergence of a scaling of the deviation of the SFS from its first-order limit. We provide a central limit theorem at both large detection times and sizes. Then, we apply these results to obtain confidence intervals for a class of consistent estimators for the fitness advance.

title: Probe Before You Edit: Probing-Guided Molecular Optimization for LLM Agents in Structure-Based Drug Design
abstract: Structure-based drug design increasingly employs LLM agents to iteratively refine ligands against a target pocket, yet a viable ligand must satisfy two often-conflicting objectives---binding affinity and druggability---which single optimization steps rarely improve together. To quantify this difficulty, we introduce two diagnostic metrics: the first measures how often a single edit improves both objectives, and the second measures how often a gain on one objective comes with a loss on the other. Applying these diagnostics to current LLM-agent pipelines exposes a consistent failure mode: the agent performs molecular editing without knowing how the pocket-ligand complex responds to local modifications, thus rarely achieving joint improvement. Inspired by medicinal chemists, who probe the pocket-ligand complex with controlled analog edits before choosing an optimization direction, we propose \textbf{PROBE}, an optimization framework built around edit--response probing. PROBE first decomposes the ligand into editable sites and builds a pocket-specific \textbf{site map} that flags where joint gains are plausible, where the two objectives are likely in tension, and where liability substructures should be changed; it then performs controlled probe edits whose responses are distilled into an \textbf{EditManual}. Guided by the site map and EditManual, PROBE runs an iterative multi-agent optimization loop. On the CrossDocked2020 benchmark, PROBE achieves state-of-the-art performance and substantially mitigates the failure modes exposed by our diagnostics metrics. Codes are in https://github.com/yzf-code/PROBE/tree/main

title: Multilevel Stochastic Plug-and-Play for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction
abstract: Sparse-view computed tomography (SVCT) reduces radiation exposure and acquisition time, but the limited number of projection views makes the reconstruction problem severely ill-posed and leads to streak artifacts when analytical methods are used. Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods combine data fidelity with learned image priors, while stochastic PnP methods use re-noising to reduce the mismatch between denoiser training inputs and reconstruction iterates. However, these methods often require many iterations, which limits their practical efficiency. In this work, we propose multilevel (ML) Stochastic Plug-and-Play (ML-SPnP), a ML stochastic PnP method for SVCT reconstruction formulated on wavelet multiresolution analysis (MRA) approximation spaces. The method combines coarse-to-fine initialization with a finite sequence of ML corrections using resolution-specific denoisers. Under suitable assumptions, the fine-level iterations following the finite ML phase inherit the convergence guarantees of the underlying stochastic PnP algorithm. Experiments on two CT datasets with 20-50 projection views show that ML-SPnP achieves reconstruction quality comparable to the evaluated stochastic PnP methods, while generally requiring less reconstruction time. These results support ML acceleration as an effective strategy for reducing the computational cost of stochastic PnP reconstruction. The code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/antoinedepaepe/ml-spnp.

title: ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators
abstract: State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory.

title: A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens
abstract: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a new interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al., 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable to the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens, and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features -- directions that act like leading, spatially coherent Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a ``Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical applied to both model classes. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens . We also introduce of a family of J-lenses built to emphasize different temporal scales of information processing in LLMs, which we call $ω$-J-lenses.

title: Attractor-Vascular Coupling Theory: Formal Grounding and Empirical Validation for AAMI-Standard Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation from Smartphone Photoplethysmography
abstract: We present Attractor-Vascular Coupling Theory (AVCT), a theory-guided framework for deriving interpretable blood pressure (BP) predictors from photoplethysmography (PPG) attractor geometry. AVCT connects vascular dynamics, PPG observation, delay-coordinate reconstruction, and attractor descriptors within a unified framework for formulating testable hypotheses, without presupposing the physiological sufficiency of a particular low-dimensional feature set. We evaluate a LightGBM-based estimator using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV) across two complementary experimental settings. Experiment 1 comprises 46 ICU/surgical subjects from BIDMC and VitalDB, with ECG, PPG, and repeated reference BP measurements. The calibrated full model achieves systolic/diastolic BP (SBP/DBP) mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 2.05/1.67 mmHg, compared with 2.02/1.63 mmHg for the PPG-attractor-only model. Experiment 2 includes 217 ambulatory subjects from the PPG-BP dataset (651 PPG windows; one cuff-based BP reference per subject) and assesses cross-subject calibrated BP reconstruction rather than within-subject BP tracking. The PPG-attractor model achieves SBP/DBP MAEs of 1.98/0.96 mmHg. Across both cohorts, incorporating ECG-derived features provides no practically meaningful improvement in MAE. Calibration substantially reduces between-subject offset error, while morphological and dynamical descriptors contribute complementary predictive information. Although the reported numerical errors fall within commonly cited thresholds associated with AAMI/ISO and BHS criteria, these findings do not establish compliance with device-validation standards. Collectively, the results support AVCT as a mechanistically motivated representation framework for interpretable PPG-based BP estimation and provide a foundation for prospective validation using repeated reference BP measurements and smartphone-acquired PPG.
